job.style: a conversation between a teacher and two students

response.passage: Teacher: Today, let us refine our geometry skills. Remember, a line segment has a fixed length, while a line extends infinitely. When measuring a segment starting at the 1 cm mark and ending at the 6 cm mark, you must subtract the start from the end to get 5 cm. Rahul: I am confused about triangles. Can I build one with sides 3 cm, 4 cm, and 7 cm? Teacher: No, Rahul. The sum of any two sides must be strictly greater than the third side. Here, 3 plus 4 equals 7, so they cannot meet to form a triangle. Priya: What about constructing a perpendicular bisector? Can I use any compass opening? Teacher: You must use a radius greater than half the segment length to ensure the arcs intersect. Also, remember that a perpendicular bisector is not just any line through the midpoint; it must be at a 90-degree angle. Finally, to construct a triangle using SAS, the angle must be placed exactly between the two given sides. If you place it elsewhere, you are not following the SAS rule. Always check your steps carefully to ensure your constructions are geometrically accurate and follow these fundamental rules.
response.summary: This passage explains how to measure line segments correctly and identifies the rules for constructing triangles. It also clarifies the requirements for drawing perpendicular bisectors and using the SAS construction method.

items.evidence: When measuring a segment starting at the 1 cm mark and ending at the 6 cm mark, you must subtract the start from the end to get 5 cm.
items.stem: What is the actual length of a segment that starts at 1 cm and ends at 6 cm?

options.why: Student ignores the starting point and reads the end mark.
Student incorrectly assumes a segment has infinite length.
Student guesses a random value unrelated to the calculation.

items.evidence: Here, 3 plus 4 equals 7, so they cannot meet to form a triangle.
items.stem: Why can sides of 3 cm, 4 cm, and 7 cm not form a triangle?

options.why: Student incorrectly believes equality satisfies the triangle inequality.
Student assumes any three lengths can form a triangle.
Student confuses side lengths with angle properties.

items.evidence: You must use a radius greater than half the segment length to ensure the arcs intersect.
items.stem: What radius is required for the compass when drawing a perpendicular bisector?

options.why: Student believes any random radius will work.
Student focuses on the midpoint rather than the radius.
Student thinks both arcs must be a specific length.

items.evidence: Finally, to construct a triangle using SAS, the angle must be placed exactly between the two given sides.
items.stem: Where must the angle be located in an SAS construction?

options.why: Student believes the angle can be at any vertex.
Student confuses SAS with right triangle hypotenuse rules.
Student incorrectly relates angle size to arm length.
